content: The simple stain is a microbiological technique used to apply color to microbial cells, making them visible under a microscope. Cells are naturally transparent or translucent, which makes them difficult to observe under a standard light microscope without the application of a staining method. In the simple staining procedure, a small sample of microbial cells is taken from a culture or growth medium and dispersed onto a single drop of water placed on a clean glass slide. The slide is then left to air dry for approximately 5 to 10 minutes, or until all the liquid has evaporated. Once dried, the slide is briefly passed over a flame with the cell side facing upward. This process, known as heat fixation, helps the cells adhere more securely to the glass surface. A dye solution, such as crystal violet, safranin, or a similar stain, is then applied to the slide, flooding the surface to cover the cells completely. The dye is allowed to remain in contact with the cells for one to two minutes before being rinsed or washed off. These dyes are particularly effective for staining bacteria because they contain positively charged (cationic) chromophores, which interact well with the negatively charged components of bacterial cells. After the staining process, the slide is allowed to dry. It can then be examined under a light or bright-field optical microscope, enabling the observation and study of the stained cells.
